memory_update.text: AI should be tracked as a multi-layer infrastructure and automation theme: demand begins with hyperscaler and enterprise AI workloads, then propagates into semiconductors, memory, packaging, networking, power/cooling, grid, and software monetization.

HBM, CoWoS-like advanced packaging, leading-edge foundry capacity, EUV lithography, optical/Ethernet networking, liquid cooling, and grid interconnection are the initial chokepoint candidates for the AI theme funnel.
Enterprise AI software is a monetization validation layer; key bottlenecks are data readiness, governance, integration, security, and ROI rather than model availability alone.
Next layer should add market-pricing checks, revenue exposure estimates, backlog/capacity evidence, and falsification metrics before any candidate ranking.
Need a component-level deep dive into data-center power equipment and cooling because AI deployment may be increasingly constrained by local grid and thermal limits rather than only chip supply.

summary: Layer 1A decomposes AI as a system-expansion theme rather than a single-ticker story. The theme splits into six investable research lanes: hyperscaler/cloud capex demand, AI accelerators plus HBM memory, advanced foundry/packaging and lithography capacity, AI data-center networking, power/cooling/grid infrastructure, and enterprise AI software/data integration. The strongest chokepoint hypotheses are not simply 'more AI apps' but physical constraints: HBM supply, advanced packaging/foundry capacity, high-end lithography lead times, data-center power interconnection, liquid cooling, and high-speed networking. Software remains important, but Layer 1A treats it as a demand validation and monetization layer that must be checked against production adoption, customer retention, and ROI evidence.

If utilization or AI monetization disappoints, the theme can reverse through order digestion.

demand_drivers: Hyperscaler cloud and AI infrastructure capex to train and serve frontier models, inference workloads, copilots, search, recommendation, enterprise AI, and AI-native applications.
Enterprise AI adoption moving from experimentation to production, increasing demand for cloud compute, data platforms, governance, workflow automation, and model-serving infrastructure.
AI server density growth, which raises requirements for GPUs/ASICs, HBM, advanced packaging, networking bandwidth, rack power, liquid cooling, backup power, and grid interconnection.
Sovereign AI, defense AI, and regulated-industry adoption, which can favor secure cloud, private AI stacks, data integration platforms, and domestically qualified supply chains.
Second-order demand from data-center siting: electrical equipment, power generation, transmission, substations, UPS, thermal systems, water/heat management, and construction services.
theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Start from the demand owner rather than the stock: hyperscaler capex disclosures, AI cloud growth, enterprise adoption, and model/inference usage. Then map into scarce layers: accelerator designers, HBM suppliers, foundry and advanced packaging, lithography and semiconductor equipment, optical/Ethernet networking, data-center power/cooling, utilities/grid services, and enterprise AI software platforms. For each public asset, verify: revenue exposure to the specific node, customer concentration, capacity expansion evidence, backlog/orders, gross margin behavior, qualification status, capex intensity, cycle risk, and whether the market already prices the bottleneck.
supply_side_constraints: HBM and advanced DRAM capacity are constrained by wafer allocation, long qualification cycles with accelerator vendors, and packaging/test complexity.
Advanced packaging such as CoWoS-like 2.5D/3D integration can bottleneck AI accelerator shipments even when wafer starts are available.
Leading-edge foundry and EUV/High-NA lithography capacity require multi-year capex, specialized suppliers, customer prepayments, and long tool lead times.
AI data centers create large, concentrated, and fast-ramping power loads; interconnection queues, substation equipment, transformers, switchgear, and local permitting can limit deployment.
High-density AI racks require liquid cooling, power distribution, thermal engineering, and facility redesign; not all legacy data centers can be upgraded economically.
Enterprise AI software faces a non-physical bottleneck: data readiness, security, governance, workflow redesign, and measurable ROI.
